etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English sirup, from Old French sirop, from Medieval Latin siruppus, syrupus, from Arabic شَرَاب (šarāb, “a drink, beverage, wine, coffee, syrup”), from شَرِبَ (šariba, “to drink”). Doublet of sirop. Related to sorbet, sherbet, sharbat. Compare French sirop, Italian siroppo, sciroppo, Spanish jarabe, jarope, Portuguese xarope, and Dutch siroop and stroop.

The first known use of the spelling sirup was in the 14th century.

definitions.definition: Any thick liquid that has a high sugar content and which is added to or poured over food as a flavouring.

quote.citation: 1819, John Keats, “The Eve of St. Agnes”, in Lamia, Isabella, the Eve of St. Agnes, and Other Poems, London:  […]  [Thomas Davison] for Taylor and Hessey, […], published 1820, →OCLC, stanza XXX, page 98:
quote.text: With jellies soother than the creamy curd, / And lucent syrops, tinct with cinnamon; [...]

quote.citation: 1990, Wayne Jancik, The Billboard Book of One-Hit Wonders, →ISBN, page 266:
quote.text: Eventually, he or his staunch public tired of his easy-listening syrup, so Price recorded gospel for the Myrrh label before semi-retiring to his Golden Cross Ranch in Texas.

definitions.definition: (Cockney rhyming slang, shortened from "syrup of figs") A wig.
(transitive) To convert or process into syrup.
(transitive) To sabotage (a vehicle) by pouring syrup into the gas tank.
